title: Filling in for George Hillman in Curly McDimple
summary: Green says he formed the Hoofers; he took over the Bojangles role for two weeks in the off-Broadway musical Curly McDimple at the Bert Wheeler Theater for George Hillman.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Chuck and Chuckles. Well, he was pinch-hitting for a vacation -- a very dear friend of his, one of the brothers of the Hillman Brothers, you see and Chris's brother. His name was George, you know. George Hillman. And he was playing Bill Bojangles Robinson, you see. But he was only playing Bill and Curly McDimple, you see.
So, he had a -- I think he had a two week vacation coming up, you know. So, he wanted someone to -- that could do script, you understand --

Yeah, you see. So, Robert Dahdah, he was known as Bob. And -- but everyone liked to called him Dardo because he was like, you know. And he had a coauthor, a lady named Marilyn, you know -- Mary Boyington. And they wrote this play called 'Curly McDimple,' and it was doing into its third year, you see, in the Burt Wheeler Theater there, (unintelligible) and Woolsey you know. (Laughter)

So, I had to laugh, see, because they had a Bill Bojangles Robinson character was featured in that, similar about -- he and Shirley McDimple. Shirley McDimple is like a little -- what do you call them when they leave the baby in the baskets, you know?

Yeah, abandoned. And she was such a -- whatcha call this -- such a loving baby, you know, a loving child, you know. She had a way of impressing people you know. But in the story of the play, Curly McDimple, it was situated someone left this basket on this boarding house, you see. And they rang the bell. And the leading man, which is a great artist -- artistic tap dancer -- Don Emmons -- he was playing in it. And I think he and George Hillman were the choreographers of this Curly McDimple.

And George Hillman was playing Bill, you know. And they had -- when she sang she -- the landlord was coming around there giving this landlady a hard time about the rents or something, you know, paying the bills, paying the expenses, you see.

So, the leading man, he says -- after the landlady come in and excusing, you know, he said that he hadn't made it, you know. He was trying to get on Broadway and get in a play or something like the Palace Theater or something there. And -- well, anyhow I got the role, playing the role of Bill and -- for the two weeks vacation. And the next thing I know was (unintelligible) saying, you know, that the newspapers said they don't come around, they don't come in and see the show and write about it, you know. It could help the -- it would help the finances more if they would come in, you know, write
about "Curly McDimple," you know what I mean. That's -- I think that's almost as long as "My Fair Lady." I mean that's going into the third year, you see.

Well anyhow, Ed Arnold was doing six nights, you know, six days, you see. And we had a Monday -- a Monday but the rent was going on, see. And I'm tickled about it, see, because it was such a happy show. It was family story show, "Curley Mc Dimple." And they was selling records, you know. And the way she sang, you know -- the baby singing, you know. And she sang, and she was going down -- way down in a bass voice, you see.

I was doing a number -- a song in the show called "Whenever raindrops started to fall, here in my heart I hear the call. A call for every Joey and Jane, I go dancing in the rain," you see. So, that's what we did.
